name: Passionflower / chamomile tea

lead: Passionflower and chamomile tea is an herbal infusion drunk before bed for relaxation and sleep. Chamomile is the better known; passionflower is often blended in. People treat the wind-down and better sleep as support for rested skin and looks.

Both plants contain flavonoids such as apigenin, which proponents link to calming effects. Encyclopedic sources say there is no good clinical evidence for chamomile in insomnia, though its anti-anxiety potential is under preliminary research, and a 2013 review of passionflower reports a good safety profile. Combination products have been tested in at least one small registered trial.

paras: It is a cup or two of tea in the evening, brewed from dried flowers or tea bags, as part of a wind-down routine. It is often paired with other sleep habits.

Chamomile can cause allergic reactions, particularly in people sensitive to daisy-family plants, and may interact with some drugs. Passionflower may add to sedatives and anticoagulants. Pregnancy use is generally flagged for medical advice.

angle.text: People drink this traditional herbal tea before bed to unwind and sleep, a routine tied to rested skin and a fresher look. Reference sources describe limited clinical evidence for sleep; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Passionflower and chamomile tea is a bedtime herbal infusion that people drink to wind down and sleep better. In appearance and physique communities the point is sleep: people who want clearer-looking skin, less tired eyes and better recovery from training treat good sleep as part of looking their best, and a calming tea is one of the routines used to get there. Chamomile tea is made from the dried flowers of German or Roman chamomile [1], and passionflower (Passiflora incarnata, or maypop) is a plant whose dried aerial parts are listed in the European and British Pharmacopoeias [2].

Research on the two herbs is uneven. A 2011 double-blind crossover study in 41 healthy adults found sleep quality rated significantly better after a week of passionflower tea than after placebo, which the authors described as initial evidence of short-term subjective benefit [3]. A 2020 randomised trial in adults with insomnia disorder reported significantly longer total sleep time with a passionflower extract than placebo on polysomnography, while other measures improved over time without differing from placebo [4]. A systematic review of nine passionflower trials covering stress, anxiety and sleep reported generally favourable effects over trials lasting one to 30 days [5].

Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence that chamomile treats any disease, that its anti-anxiety potential is under preliminary research, and that there is no good evidence for insomnia [1]. Reviews of herbal sleep aids describe interactions with the GABA system as a proposed route for sedative effects [6].
infobox: Chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla or Chamaemelum nobile); Passiflora incarnata

paras: Chamomile flowers contain flavonoids and polyphenols including apigenin, quercetin and luteolin [1]. Passionflower contains flavonoids such as chrysin, apigenin, luteolin and quercetin, plus alkaloids, with the highest flavonoid concentration in the leaves [2].

Chamomile and passionflower are sold as single-herb teas and as blends, often alongside lemon balm or valerian. On T Nation, lifters describe alternating chamomile and passionflower tea at night, adding passionflower tea before bed, or taking tea with melatonin as part of a wind-down routine [7][8][9]. One lifter says passionflower extract takes the edge off without the melatonin 'hangover' [10]. Another notes the routine itself, not only the herbs, may be what helps [11].

A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of 41 healthy adults found that passionflower tea gave significantly better sleep-quality ratings than placebo, with polysomnography in ten participants [3].

In adults with insomnia disorder, a double-blind placebo-controlled study of Passiflora incarnata reported a significant increase in total sleep time versus placebo (P = 0.049); sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset improved within the group but did not differ from placebo [4].

A pilot double-blind trial in 36 outpatients with generalised anxiety compared passionflower extract with oxazepam over four weeks and found no significant difference, with less job-performance impairment on passionflower [12]. A 2020 systematic review of nine passionflower trials and a 2022 network meta-analysis of medicinal herbs for anxiety are further sources [5][13]. A registered phase 1 trial (2019, 27 participants) tested a herbal formula, Rest-ZZZ, in healthy adults with difficulty sleeping [14].

Chamomile may interact with some herbs and drugs, may worsen pollen allergies, and can cause reactions in people allergic to daisies, ragweed and related plants; Roman chamomile may cause uterine contractions and is advised against in pregnancy [1]. Passionflower may increase the effect of sedatives, anticoagulants and MAO inhibitors, and pregnant or breastfeeding women are advised to consult a professional [2].

lore.intro: Chamomile and passionflower tea come up in strength-training forums as non-drug options for winding down before bed.

claims.claim: Passionflower tea or extract helps you fall asleep without the melatonin 'hangover'.
The ritual of a warm drink matters as much as the herbs.
